column9: When potassium and fluorine bond, electrons are transferred rather than shared.
column28: True. Potassium is a metal and fluorine is a nonmetal, so they form an ionic bond: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal.
column29: Is potassium a metal or a nonmetal? Is fluorine?

column9: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
column14: To lose all of their electrons
column28: Atoms bond to be stable, usually by getting 8 electrons in their outer shell. Bonding does not change which element an atom is.
column29: Think about the octet rule. What do atoms get when their outer shell is full?

column9: By the octet rule, most atoms are stable when they have ___ electrons in their outer shell.
column28: Octet means 8. Most elements are stable with 8 outer electrons; hydrogen and helium are the exceptions.
column29: Noble gases like neon already have this many outer electrons.

column9: Magnesium and oxygen bond to form a compound. What happens to the electrons?
column17: No electrons move; the atoms just stick
column28: Mg is a metal and O is a nonmetal, so the bond is ionic: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal. Sharing happens only between nonmetals.
column29: Is this metal + nonmetal or nonmetal + nonmetal? Then: which one gives electrons away?

column9: Dev says neon does not form compounds because it is a gas. Rae says neon does not form compounds because its outer shell is already full. Who has the stronger argument?
column14: Both, because every gas has a full outer shell
column15: Dev, because gases never form bonds
column16: Rae, because a full outer shell means neon is already stable
column17: Neither, because neon bonds easily with metals
column28: Atoms bond to become stable. Neon is a noble gas whose outer shell is already full, so it has no reason to bond. Dev's reason fails: oxygen and carbon dioxide are gases that have bonds.
column29: Why do atoms bond in the first place? Does neon need to?

column9: Which phrase describes what happens to electrons in an ionic bond?
column14: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another
column15: Electrons are shared between two atoms
column16: Neutrons move from one atom to another
column17: Protons are shared between two atoms
column28: In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred: the metal gives them and the nonmetal takes them. Sharing electrons is a covalent bond. Protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus.
column29: Think of the lunch money analogy: one person hands a dollar to another.

column9: Which group of elements already has a full outer shell, so its atoms almost never form compounds?
column28: Noble gases like neon and argon already have a full outer shell, so they are already stable and have no reason to bond. Groups 1 and 17 bond very easily.
column29: Atoms bond to become stable. Which group is already stable?

column9: An atom or group of atoms that has a positive or negative charge is called an ___.
column28: A charged atom or group of atoms is an ion. Metals form positive ions and nonmetals form negative ions, and ionic compounds are made of ions.
column29: It is the first part of the word ionic.

column9: When an ionic bond forms, which kind of element gives away electrons?
column28: In an ionic bond, the metal gives electrons away and becomes a positive ion; the nonmetal takes them and becomes a negative ion. Sharing happens only in covalent bonds.
column29: Metals are the givers and nonmetals are the takers.

column9: Group 1 metals bond with Group 17 nonmetals (like K with Cl). What kind of compounds do they form?
column15: Ionic: the metal transfers an electron to the nonmetal
column16: None: both groups are already stable
column17: Ionic: the nonmetal transfers electrons to the metal
column28: Group 1 elements are metals and Group 17 elements are nonmetals, so they form ionic compounds: the metal gives its electron to the nonmetal. Neither group is already stable (that is Group 18).
column29: Which group is the giver, and which is the taker?

column9: A chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons. How does it become stable when it bonds with sodium?
column14: It loses all 7 of its outer electrons
column28: Most atoms are stable with 8 outer electrons. Chlorine needs just 1 more, so it takes 1 electron from sodium (a metal) and becomes Cl⁻. That transfer is an ionic bond.
column29: How many more electrons does chlorine need to reach 8?

column9: How does an ionic bond form?
column14: Two metal atoms share all of their electrons
column15: Two nonmetal atoms share pairs of electrons
column17: A metal atom transfers electrons to a nonmetal atom, and the opposite charges attract
column28: In an ionic bond a metal gives valence electrons to a nonmetal. The metal becomes a positive ion, the nonmetal becomes a negative ion, and the opposite charges attract. Sharing electrons is a covalent bond.
column29: Think of handing a friend a dollar: one gives and one takes.

column9: An atom that LOSES electrons becomes an ion with a ___ charge.
column28: Electrons are negative. An atom that loses electrons has more protons than electrons, so its charge is positive.
column29: Electrons are negative. What is left over when you take negatives away?

column9: An atom that GAINS electrons becomes an ion with a ___ charge.
column28: Electrons are negative. An atom that gains electrons has more electrons than protons, so its charge is negative.
column29: Electrons are negative. What happens to the charge when you add more of them?

column9: In an ionic bond, the nonmetal atom gains the electrons that the metal atom loses.
column28: True. The metal is the giver and the nonmetal is the taker. Electrons are not destroyed; they move from the metal to the nonmetal.
column29: Which kind of element is the giver, and which is the taker?

column9: Sodium has 1 valence electron. What does a sodium atom do when it forms an ionic bond?
column14: It gains 7 electrons and becomes Na⁷⁻
column15: It shares 1 electron with another sodium atom
column16: It loses 1 electron and becomes Na⁺
column17: It gains 1 electron and becomes Na⁻
column28: Losing 1 electron is much easier than gaining 7. With 1 fewer electron than protons, sodium becomes Na⁺.
column29: Is it easier to lose 1 electron or gain 7?

column9: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons. Which ion does a chlorine atom form in an ionic bond?
column28: Chlorine needs just 1 more electron to reach 8, so it gains 1. One extra electron gives a charge of 1−: Cl⁻.
column29: How many more electrons does chlorine need to reach 8?

column9: Magnesium is in Group 2. How many valence electrons does a magnesium atom lose when it forms an ion?
column28: Group 2 metals have 2 valence electrons and lose both, forming a 2+ ion: Mg²⁺.
column29: For Groups 1 and 2, the group number is the number of valence electrons.

column9: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. How many electrons does an oxygen atom gain to fill its outer level?
column28: Oxygen needs 8 outer electrons: 8 − 6 = 2. Gaining 2 electrons makes the oxide ion, O²⁻.
column29: Most atoms are stable with 8 outer electrons. How far is 6 from 8?

column9: What holds the ions together in an ionic compound?
column14: The attraction between positive ions and negative ions
column16: The attraction between the neutrons of each atom
column17: Pairs of electrons shared between the atoms
column28: Opposite charges attract. After the electrons move, the positive metal ions and negative nonmetal ions pull on each other. That attraction is the ionic bond.
column29: What do a + charge and a − charge do to each other?

column9: Why does a calcium atom lose 2 electrons instead of gaining 6?
column14: Calcium is a nonmetal, and nonmetals always lose electrons
column17: Losing 2 is easier, and it leaves a full outer level underneath
column28: Calcium has only 2 valence electrons. Losing 2 takes far less energy than gaining 6, and the level underneath is already full.
column29: Calcium is in Group 2. Which is the shorter path to a full outer level?

column9: One magnesium atom has 2 valence electrons to give away. Each chlorine atom can take only 1. How many chlorine atoms does one magnesium atom need?
column28: Magnesium gives 1 electron to each of 2 chlorine atoms. That makes one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻: MgCl₂.
column29: Each chlorine has room for just 1 more electron. Where does magnesium's second electron go?

column9: A calcium atom gives one electron to each of two fluorine atoms. Which ions form, and what is the formula?
column28: Calcium loses 2 electrons (Ca²⁺). Each fluorine gains 1 (F⁻). One Ca²⁺ balances two F⁻: CaF₂.
column29: Count how many electrons calcium lost in all, and how many each fluorine gained.

column9: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons. In an ionic bond, how many sodium atoms does one sulfur atom need so that every atom ends up with a full outer level?
column28: Sulfur needs 2 more electrons. Each sodium gives only 1, so it takes 2 sodium atoms: Na₂S.
column29: How many electrons does sulfur need? How many can one sodium give?

column9: Aluminum has 3 valence electrons and oxygen has 6. Two aluminum atoms give away all of their valence electrons. How many oxygen atoms does it take to accept them?
column28: Two aluminum atoms give 2 × 3 = 6 electrons. Each oxygen takes 2, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 oxygen atoms: Al₂O₃.
column29: First find the total electrons given away. Then divide by what one oxygen can take.

column9: When a metal atom becomes a positive ion, what has changed?
column15: It gained protons in its nucleus
column17: It lost electrons, so it now has more protons than electrons
column28: Only electrons move in bonding. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive.
column29: Bonding only involves the outside of the atom. Which particles are out there?

column9: When a sodium atom becomes Na⁺, the number of protons in its nucleus changes.
column28: False. Sodium keeps its 11 protons. It loses 1 electron, so it has 11 protons and 10 electrons: a charge of 1+.
column29: Which particles are transferred in a bond: protons or electrons?

column9: A lithium atom has 3 protons and 3 electrons. After it forms an ionic bond, it has 3 protons and 2 electrons. What is its charge?
column28: 3 protons (+3) and 2 electrons (−2) add to +1. Lithium lost one electron, so it is Li⁺.
column29: Add the charges: each proton is +1 and each electron is −1.

column9: A sulfur atom has 16 protons. As a sulfide ion it has 18 electrons. What is the ion's charge?
column28: 16 protons (+16) and 18 electrons (−18) add to −2. Sulfur gained 2 electrons, so it is S²⁻.
column29: Compare the number of electrons with the number of protons. Which is bigger, and by how much?

column9: Which particles move from one atom to another when an ionic bond forms?
column28: Only the outer (valence) electrons are involved in bonding. Protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus.
column29: Which particles are on the outside of the atom?

column9: Which pair of elements will bond by transferring electrons?
column28: Lithium is a metal and fluorine is a nonmetal, so lithium transfers an electron to fluorine. The other pairs have no metal, and neon and argon are noble gases that do not bond.
column29: Transfer needs a giver (a metal) and a taker (a nonmetal).

column9: Put the steps in order to explain how sodium and chlorine form an ionic bond.
column14: Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻
column15: A sodium atom has 1 valence electron and a chlorine atom has 7
column16: The opposite charges attract and hold the ions together
column17: Sodium transfers its 1 valence electron to chlorine
column28: Start with the valence electrons (1 and 7). Sodium transfers its electron, the atoms become the ions Na⁺ and Cl⁻, and the opposite charges attract.
column29: The ions cannot attract until they exist, and they do not exist until the electron moves.

column9: Match each atom to what it does when it forms an ionic bond. Use its group on the periodic table.
column28: Metals lose their valence electrons: Group 1 loses 1, Group 2 loses 2, Group 13 loses 3. Nonmetals gain enough to reach 8: Group 15 gains 3, Group 16 gains 2, Group 17 gains 1.
column29: Metals on the left lose electrons. Nonmetals on the right gain enough to reach 8.

column9: Maya says, "In NaCl, the sodium and chlorine atoms share an electron." Which response is best?
column14: Maya is wrong: chlorine gives an electron to sodium
column15: Maya is wrong: sodium (a metal) gives its electron to chlorine (a nonmetal), and the ions Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract
column16: Maya is right, because both atoms end up with 8 outer electrons
column17: Maya is right: all bonds form by sharing electrons
column28: A metal and a nonmetal transfer electrons. Sodium gives 1 electron to chlorine, making Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Sharing happens between two nonmetals.
column29: Is sodium a metal or a nonmetal? What do metals do with their valence electrons?

column9: Why is the formula for magnesium chloride MgCl₂ and not MgCl?
column14: The 2 is the charge on the chloride ion
column15: Chlorine atoms always come in pairs in every compound
column16: Magnesium loses 2 electrons and each chlorine can take only 1, so it takes 2 chlorines
column17: There are 2 magnesium atoms in the compound
column28: Mg loses 2 electrons to become Mg²⁺. Each Cl gains only 1 to become Cl⁻. Two Cl⁻ are needed to balance one Mg²⁺.
column29: How many electrons does magnesium give away? How many can one chlorine take?

column9: Leo draws potassium and oxygen bonding. In his drawing, one K atom gives 2 electrons to one O atom, making KO. What is wrong with his drawing?
column14: Potassium has only 1 valence electron to give, so it takes 2 K atoms: K₂O
column15: Oxygen should give 2 electrons to potassium
column16: Oxygen needs only 1 electron, so the formula should be KO₂
column17: Nothing is wrong; KO is correct
column28: Potassium is in Group 1, so each atom gives just 1 electron. Oxygen needs 2, so two potassium atoms each give 1: K₂O.
column29: Check potassium's group. How many valence electrons does one potassium atom have?

column9: Aluminum (Group 13) bonds with chlorine (Group 17). Which statement describes the electron transfer?
column14: One Cl atom gives 3 electrons to one Al atom, making AlCl
column15: One Al atom shares 3 electrons with one Cl atom, making AlCl
column16: Three Al atoms each give 1 electron to one Cl atom, making Al₃Cl
column17: One Al atom gives 1 electron to each of 3 Cl atoms, making AlCl₃
column28: Aluminum has 3 valence electrons to give. Each chlorine takes only 1, so it takes 3 chlorines: Al³⁺ and three Cl⁻ make AlCl₃.
column29: Aluminum gives away 3 electrons. How many can each chlorine take?

column9: The electron dot diagram for a sodium atom shows 1 dot. What does the dot diagram for the sodium ION look like after sodium bonds with chlorine?
column14: Na with no dots and a 1+ charge
column15: Na with 1 dot and a 1+ charge
column17: Na with 8 dots and a 1− charge
column28: Sodium gave its one valence electron away, so no dots are left and the ion has a 1+ charge: Na⁺.
column29: Dots show valence electrons. What happened to sodium's one valence electron?

column9: A chlorine atom has 7 dots in its dot diagram. After it takes an electron from sodium, how many dots does it have, and what is its charge?
column28: Chlorine gains 1 electron: 7 + 1 = 8 dots. One extra electron gives a charge of 1−: Cl⁻.
column29: Chlorine gained an electron. Does that add a dot or remove one? Is an electron + or −?

column9: An ionic compound has an overall charge of zero because its positive and negative charges cancel.
column28: True. The ions combine in a ratio where the total positive charge equals the total negative charge, like +2 and two −1 in MgCl₂.
column29: Add the charges in NaCl: +1 and −1.

column9: Why do metals tend to lose electrons instead of gaining them?
column14: They have no valence electrons at all
column16: They have more neutrons than nonmetals do
column17: They have only a few valence electrons, so losing them is the easier way to a full outer level
column28: Metals have 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons. Losing a few is easier than gaining 5 or more, and it leaves a full level underneath.
column29: Compare losing 1 or 2 electrons with gaining 6 or 7.

column9: The electrons in an atom's outer level, the ones used in bonding, are called ___ electrons.
column28: Valence electrons are the outer electrons. They are the ones lost, gained or shared when atoms bond.
column29: The dots in an electron dot diagram stand for these electrons.

column9: Element X is a metal with 2 valence electrons. Element Z is a nonmetal with 5 valence electrons. What is the formula of the ionic compound they form?
column28: X loses 2 (X²⁺). Z needs 3 more to reach 8 (Z³⁻). Three X²⁺ (+6) balance two Z³⁻ (−6): X₃Z₂.
column29: Find each ion's charge first. Z gains enough electrons to reach 8.

column9: Which of these atoms LOSE electrons when they form an ionic bond? Select all that apply.
column28: Metals lose electrons: lithium, barium and aluminum. Sulfur, bromine and oxygen are nonmetals, so they gain electrons.
column29: Metals are the givers. Which of these sit left of the staircase?

column9: Calcium has 2 valence electrons and nitrogen has 5. How many electrons in total are transferred to make one formula unit of Ca₃N₂?
column28: Three calcium atoms each lose 2: 3 × 2 = 6 electrons. Two nitrogen atoms each gain 3: 2 × 3 = 6. The numbers match.
column29: Count the electrons the 3 calcium atoms give away.

column9: Which kind of element usually forms negative ions?
column28: Nonmetals gain electrons to fill their outer level, so they form negative ions. Metals lose electrons and form positive ions.
column29: Which kind of element is the taker in an ionic bond?

column9: Magnesium is in Group 2. Which ion does magnesium form?
column28: Group 2 metals lose 2 electrons, so magnesium forms Mg²⁺. Metals make positive ions; 12 is magnesium's atomic number, not its charge.
column29: Use the group number rule: Group 1 is +1, Group 2 is +2. Are metals positive or negative?

column9: Match each element to the charge of the ion it forms. Use its group number on the periodic table.
column28: Group 1 = +1 (Na), Group 2 = +2 (Ca), Group 13 = +3 (Al), Group 15 = −3 (N), Group 16 = −2 (O, S), Group 17 = −1 (Cl). Metals are positive and nonmetals are negative.
column29: Find each element's group. Metals on the left lose electrons (+); nonmetals on the right gain electrons (−).

column9: In the finished formula for an ionic compound, the ion charges are still written as superscripts (like Ca²⁺Cl⁻₂).
column28: False. The charge drops to the bottom as a subscript on the opposite side "with no charge," so the finished formula is just CaCl₂. Charges are only written while you are setting up the ions.
column29: Look at any formula in your notes, like MgCl₂. Do you see any + or − signs in it?

column9: Sodium forms Na⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻. What is the formula for sodium chloride?
column28: Na⁺ (+1) and Cl⁻ (−1) already cancel, so one of each: NaCl. NaCl₂ and Na₂Cl do not balance, and the metal is always written first.
column29: Do +1 and −1 already add up to zero? Which element is written first?

column9: Potassium forms K⁺ and bromine forms Br⁻. Type the formula for potassium bromide: ___
column28: K⁺ is +1 and Br⁻ is −1, so +1 − 1 = 0 with one of each: KBr. No subscripts are needed when the charges already cancel.
column29: If the two charges are the same size, how many of each ion do you need?

column9: How many potassium ions (K⁺) does it take to balance the charge of one sulfide ion (S²⁻)?
column28: One S²⁻ is −2. Each K⁺ is +1, so it takes 2: 2(+1) + 1(−2) = 0. The formula for potassium sulfide is K₂S.
column29: How many +1 charges add up to cancel a −2?

column9: How many chloride ions (Cl⁻) does it take to balance the charge of one aluminum ion (Al³⁺)?
column28: One Al³⁺ is +3. Each Cl⁻ is −1, so it takes 3: 1(+3) + 3(−1) = 0.
column29: How many −1 charges add up to cancel a +3?

column9: When you criss-cross to write an ionic formula, what happens to each ion's charge number?
column14: It moves to the front of the formula as a big number (coefficient)
column15: It drops to the bottom as a subscript on the opposite ion, with no sign
column16: It is added to the other ion's charge to get the subscript
column17: It drops to the bottom as a subscript on its own ion, with its sign
column28: Crisscross: the little charge that appears as a superscript drops to the bottom of the formula as a subscript on the opposite side with no charge (Mg²⁺ P³⁻ → Mg₃P₂).
column29: Think of the "X" in criss-cross. Which ion does each charge land on?

column9: Put the steps for writing an ionic formula in order.
column14: Reduce the subscripts if they share a factor
column15: Write each ion with its charge
column16: Check that the charges add up to zero
column17: Criss-cross the charges down as subscripts on the opposite ion
column28: Write the ions with charges, criss-cross the charges down, reduce if you can, then ALWAYS double check that the charges cancel to zero.
column29: You cannot criss-cross until you know the charges, and you check your work last.

column9: Which element forms an ion with a 3− charge?
column28: Nitrogen is in Group 15, so it gains 3 electrons to make N³⁻. Aluminum is +3 (a metal loses electrons), sodium is +1, and chlorine is −1.
column29: Negative ions come from nonmetals. Which group number gives −3?

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻. The formula for barium hydroxide is Ba(OH)₂. Why are there parentheses around OH?
column14: Hydroxide is negative, and negative ions always get parentheses
column15: The parentheses show that oxygen and hydrogen are both nonmetals
column16: There are 2 hydroxide ions, and the 2 must apply to the whole ion
column17: Parentheses always go around the nonmetal part of a formula
column28: Use parentheses only when you need 2 or more of a polyatomic ion. Ba²⁺ needs two OH⁻, and the 2 outside the parentheses multiplies both O and H. With only one polyatomic ion (like KOH) there are no parentheses.
column29: What would BaOH₂ mean? Which atom would the 2 apply to?

column9: The Roman numeral in iron(III) chloride tells you there are three iron atoms in the formula.
column28: False. The Roman numeral is the CHARGE of the iron ion: iron(III) means Fe³⁺. Iron(III) bromide is FeBr₃, with only one iron.
column29: Is the Roman numeral a count of atoms or the charge of the metal ion?

column9: Type the formula for aluminum nitride: ___
column28: Al is Group 13 (Al³⁺) and N is Group 15 (N³⁻). Criss-cross gives Al₃N₃, which reduces to AlN. Check: +3 − 3 = 0.
column29: Find each charge from its group number. After you criss-cross, can the subscripts be reduced?

column9: Type the formula for aluminum oxide: ___
column28: Al³⁺ and O²⁻: criss-cross the 3 and the 2 to get Al₂O₃. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = +6 − 6 = 0.
column29: Get each charge from the group number (Group 13 and Group 16), then criss-cross.

column9: The formula for calcium nitride is Ca₃N₂. What is the total positive charge from all the calcium ions? Type just the number.
column28: Each calcium is Ca²⁺, and there are 3: 3(+2) = +6. That cancels the nitrides: 2(−3) = −6, and +6 − 6 = 0.
column29: Multiply the number of calcium ions by the charge of one calcium ion (Group 2).

column9: What is the formula for barium oxide?
column28: Ba²⁺ and O²⁻: criss-cross gives Ba₂O₂, which reduces to BaO. Check: +2 − 2 = 0. Ba₂O₂ forgot to reduce. BaO₂ and Ba₂O are not barium oxide: with Ba²⁺ and O²⁻ their charges do not cancel.
column29: Barium is Group 2 and oxygen is Group 16. After you criss-cross, can you reduce?

column9: What is the formula for potassium phosphide?
column28: K⁺ and P³⁻: criss-cross gives K₃P. Check: 3(+1) + 1(−3) = 0. KP₃ put the subscript on the wrong side; KP and K₃P₃ do not balance.
column29: Potassium is Group 1 and phosphorus is Group 15. Each charge crosses to the OTHER ion.

column9: In aluminum sulfide, how many sulfide ions (S²⁻) are there for every 2 aluminum ions (Al³⁺)?
column28: 2 Al³⁺ = 2(+3) = +6. Each S²⁻ is −2, so you need 3: 3(−2) = −6. The formula is Al₂S₃.
column29: Find the total positive charge of the 2 aluminum ions first. How many −2 charges cancel it?

column9: Write the formula for potassium nitride in your head. What is the subscript on K? Type just the number.
column28: K⁺ (Group 1) and N³⁻ (Group 15): the 3 from nitride crosses down to potassium, giving K₃N. Check: 3(+1) + 1(−3) = 0.
column29: Nitrogen's charge comes from Group 15. That number drops down onto the opposite ion.

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻. Type the formula for sodium hydroxide: ___
column28: Na⁺ (+1) and OH⁻ (−1) cancel with one of each: NaOH. You only need parentheses when there are 2 or more of a polyatomic ion.
column29: Do the charges cancel with just one of each? If so, do you need parentheses?

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. Type the formula for magnesium nitrate: ___
column28: Mg²⁺ and NO₃⁻: criss-cross the 2 onto nitrate. Protect nitrate with parentheses: Mg(NO₃)₂. Check: +2 + 2(−1) = 0. MgNO₃₂ changes the ion inside.
column29: You need more than one nitrate. Put parentheses around NO₃ and keep the subscript outside.

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺. Type the formula for ammonium chloride: ___
column28: NH₄⁺ (+1) and Cl⁻ (−1) cancel with one of each: NH₄Cl. Ammonium is the positive ion, so it goes first, and with only one there are no parentheses.
column29: Ammonium is the positive ion here, so it goes first. Do +1 and −1 already cancel?

column9: Carbonate is CO₃²⁻. What is the formula for calcium carbonate?
column28: Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ cancel with one of each: CaCO₃. Ca₂(CO₃)₂ was not reduced, Ca(CO₃)₂ does not balance (+2 − 4), and CaCO₂ changed the subscript inside the ion.
column29: Compare the two charges. If they are the same size, how many of each do you need?

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the formula for potassium sulfate?
column28: K⁺ and SO₄²⁻: the 2 crosses onto potassium, so K₂SO₄. Check: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0. KSO₄ does not balance, K(SO₄)₂ crossed the wrong way, and K₂SO₃ changed the ion.
column29: Which ion needs more than one copy to cancel a −2? Never change the subscripts inside SO₄.

column9: Type the formula for tin(II) bromide: ___
column28: Tin(II) means Sn²⁺; bromide is Br⁻ (Group 17). Criss-cross: SnBr₂. Check: +2 + 2(−1) = 0.
column29: The Roman numeral is the charge on tin. Then criss-cross like any other ionic compound.

column9: What is the formula for lead(IV) oxide?
column28: Lead(IV) is Pb⁴⁺ and oxide is O²⁻. Criss-cross gives Pb₂O₄, which reduces to PbO₂. Check: +4 + 2(−2) = 0. PbO₄ used the Roman numeral as a subscript.
column29: The IV is lead's charge. Criss-cross the 4 and the 2, then reduce.

column9: What is the subscript on Cu in the formula for copper(I) sulfide? Type just the number.
column28: Copper(I) is Cu⁺ and sulfide is S²⁻. The 2 crosses onto copper: Cu₂S. Check: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0. The I is the charge, not the number of copper atoms.
column29: Use the Roman numeral as copper's charge and sulfur's group for its charge, then criss-cross.

column9: Select every formula that is valid (the charges cancel to zero). Select all that apply.
column29: For each formula, multiply each subscript by its ion's charge and add. Valid ones add to zero.

column9: Match each ionic compound to its correct formula.
column28: Na⁺ + O²⁻ → Na₂O; Ca²⁺ + F⁻ → CaF₂; Rb⁺ + Cl⁻ → RbCl; Sr²⁺ + Br⁻ → SrBr₂; Li⁺ + I⁻ → LiI. Each one's charges add to zero.
column29: Get each charge from its group number, criss-cross, and check that the charges cancel.

column9: Calcium always forms a 2+ ion, so a calcium compound like calcium bromide does not need a Roman numeral in its name.
column28: True. Group 1, 2, and 13 metals always have the same charge (calcium is always +2), so there is nothing to specify. Only metals that can have more than one charge (like Fe, Cu, Pb, Sn) get a Roman numeral.
column29: Does calcium ever have a charge other than the one its group gives it?

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Type the formula for iron(III) sulfate: ___
column28: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Criss-cross: Fe₂(SO₄)₃. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Keep SO₄ in parentheses and do not change anything inside.
column29: Two steps: the Roman numeral gives iron's charge, then criss-cross and protect the polyatomic ion with parentheses.

column9: Dev says copper(II) chloride is CuCl because there is only one copper. Rae says it is CuCl₂. Which choice gives the stronger argument?
column14: Dev: the name says one copper and one chlorine, so CuCl is right
column15: Dev: copper is a metal, so it always forms a +1 ion
column16: Rae: the II in the name means there are two chlorine atoms
column17: Rae: the II means Cu²⁺, and it takes two Cl⁻ ions to cancel +2
column28: Rae is right for the right reason: the Roman numeral is copper's charge (+2), and +2 + 2(−1) = 0, so CuCl₂. The choice "the II means two chlorine atoms" has the right formula but the wrong reason; Dev used the number of copper atoms as its charge.
column29: What does the Roman numeral stand for? A strong argument needs the right answer AND the right reason.

column9: Sam says iron(III) oxide is FeO₃ "because it says three." Which choice gives the correct formula and explains Sam's mistake?
column14: Fe₂O₃; the III is iron's charge, so criss-cross Fe³⁺ and O²⁻
column15: Fe₃O₂; the III tells you there are three iron atoms
column16: FeO₃; the III tells you there are three oxygen atoms
column17: Fe₃O₃; the III goes on both iron and oxygen
column28: The Roman numeral is the charge, not a subscript. Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ criss-cross to Fe₂O₃: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. FeO₃ would be +3 − 6, which does not cancel.
column29: Use the Roman numeral as iron's charge and find oxygen's charge from its group. Then check that the charges cancel.

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. Type the formula for lead(II) nitrate: ___
column28: Lead(II) is Pb²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻. The 2 crosses onto nitrate: Pb(NO₃)₂. Check: +2 + 2(−1) = 0.
column29: The II is lead's charge. You need more than one nitrate, so think about parentheses.

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Type the formula for ammonium phosphate: ___
column28: NH₄⁺ and PO₄³⁻: the 3 crosses onto ammonium, so (NH₄)₃PO₄. Check: 3(+1) + (−3) = 0. NH₄₃PO₄ is wrong because it changes the ion instead of tripling it.
column29: Both ions are polyatomic. Which one do you need more than one of? That one gets parentheses.

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻. Type the formula for aluminum hydroxide: ___
column28: Al³⁺ and OH⁻: the 3 crosses onto hydroxide, giving Al(OH)₃. Check: +3 + 3(−1) = 0. AlOH₃ would mean 3 hydrogens but only 1 oxygen.
column29: Aluminum's charge comes from Group 13. If you need more than one hydroxide, protect it with parentheses.

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the formula for tin(IV) sulfate?
column28: Tin(IV) is Sn⁴⁺. Criss-cross with SO₄²⁻ gives Sn₂(SO₄)₄, which reduces to Sn(SO₄)₂ (reduce only the subscripts outside the parentheses). Check: +4 + 2(−2) = 0.
column29: Criss-cross the 4 and the 2, then see whether the outside subscripts can be reduced.

column9: Acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻. In the formula for iron(III) acetate, what number goes outside the parentheses? Type just the number.
column28: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and acetate is −1, so it takes 3 acetates: Fe(C₂H₃O₂)₃. Check: +3 + 3(−1) = 0.
column29: The Roman numeral gives iron's charge. How many −1 ions cancel it?

column9: Use these ions: chlorate ClO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺. Select every formula that is written correctly. Select all that apply.
column28: Correct: Ca(ClO₃)₂, Al₂(CO₃)₃, K₃PO₄ (charges cancel, parentheses only when 2 or more). NaSO₄ does not balance (should be Na₂SO₄), Ca₂(PO₄)₃ crossed the wrong way (should be Ca₃(PO₄)₂), and NH₄₂SO₄ is missing parentheses (should be (NH₄)₂SO₄).
column29: For each one: do the charges cancel, did the charges cross to the opposite ion, and are parentheses used when there are 2 or more of a polyatomic ion?

column9: Select every name that is matched with its correct formula. Select all that apply.
column28: Correct: PbO (+2 − 2), FeCl₃ (+3 + 3(−1)), SnCl₄ (+4 + 4(−1)). Copper(II) oxide is CuO (CuO₂ used the numeral as a subscript), lead(II) bromide is PbBr₂ (Pb₂Br crossed the wrong way), and iron(II) sulfide is FeS (Fe₂S₂ was not reduced).
column29: Use each Roman numeral as the metal's charge, criss-cross, reduce, and compare.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Maya and Leo both wrote Pb₃(PO₄)₄ for lead(IV) phosphate. Which justification is strongest?
column14: Lead(IV) is Pb⁴⁺; criss-cross gives Pb₃(PO₄)₄, and it should be reduced to Pb(PO₄)
column15: Lead is a metal and phosphate is polyatomic, so lead is always written first
column16: Lead(IV) is Pb⁴⁺ and phosphate is −3; criss-cross gives Pb₃(PO₄)₄, and 3(+4) + 4(−3) = 0
column17: The name has a IV, so there must be 4 phosphates, and lead gets the 3 left over
column28: The strongest justification gives each charge (Pb⁴⁺, PO₄³⁻), criss-crosses, and checks that the charges cancel: 3(+4) = +12 and 4(−3) = −12. 3 and 4 share no factor, so it cannot be reduced. Writing the metal first is true but does not explain the subscripts.
column29: A strong justification uses the charges AND shows the charge check. Which choice does both without a wrong step?

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. How many phosphate ions are in one formula unit of manganese(II) phosphate? Type just the number.
column28: Manganese(II) is Mn²⁺ and phosphate is −3. Criss-cross: Mn₃(PO₄)₂, so 2 phosphate ions. Check: 3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0.
column29: Use the II as manganese's charge and criss-cross. The charge of manganese becomes phosphate's subscript.

column9: Acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻. Type the formula for copper(II) acetate: ___
column28: Copper(II) is Cu²⁺ and acetate is −1, so it takes 2 acetates: Cu(C₂H₃O₂)₂. Check: +2 + 2(−1) = 0. Do not change the 2, 3, 2 inside acetate.
column29: Find copper's charge from the numeral. Protect the whole acetate ion with parentheses if you need more than one.

column9: Oxygen is in Group 16. What is the charge on an oxide ion?
column28: Group 16 nonmetals gain 2 electrons, so oxygen forms O²⁻. Nonmetals make negative ions; 8 is oxygen's atomic number, not its charge.
column29: Group 15 = −3, Group 16 = −2, Group 17 = −1. Are nonmetal ions positive or negative?

column9: Which pair of ions has charges that already cancel with just one of each?
column28: +1 and −1 add to zero, so one Na⁺ and one Br⁻ make NaBr. Each other pair has charges of different sizes, so it needs more than one of at least one ion.
column29: Add the two charges in each pair. Which pair adds to exactly zero?

column9: Which statement about ions is true?
column14: Both metals and nonmetals form positive ions
column15: Metals form negative ions and nonmetals form positive ions
column17: Metals form positive ions and nonmetals form negative ions
column28: Metals lose electrons, so they become positive ions (like Na⁺). Nonmetals gain electrons, so they become negative ions (like Cl⁻).
column29: Metals give electrons away. Does losing negative electrons leave a + or − charge?

column9: In the formula for an ionic compound, which ion is written first?
column28: The metal (positive ion) always goes first, just like in the name: sodium chloride is NaCl, not ClNa.
column29: Look at the name sodium chloride. Which part is said first?

column9: Lithium fluoride is used in special lenses. Lithium is Li⁺ and fluoride is F⁻. Choose its formula.
column28: Li⁺ (+1) and F⁻ (−1) already cancel, so the formula is one of each: LiF. LiF₂ and Li₂F do not balance, and the metal is written first.
column29: Do +1 and −1 already add to zero? Which symbol goes first?

column9: Cesium is Cs⁺ and iodine forms I⁻. What is the formula of cesium iodide? Type it here: ___
column28: Cs⁺ is +1 and I⁻ is −1, so one of each cancels: CsI. Remember the capital C and lowercase s for cesium.
column29: Equal-size charges mean one of each ion. Watch the capital and lowercase letters in the symbols.

column9: One Ba²⁺ ion needs how many Br⁻ ions so the charges add up to zero?
column28: Ba²⁺ is +2. Each Br⁻ is −1, so it takes 2: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. The formula is BaBr₂.
column29: How many −1 charges does it take to cancel +2?

column9: A nitride ion, N³⁻, has a charge of −3. How many Na⁺ ions add up to +3 to cancel it?
column28: Each Na⁺ is +1, so 3 of them give +3: 3(+1) + (−3) = 0. The formula for sodium nitride is Na₃N.
column29: How many +1 charges add up to +3?

column9: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ combine. Which formula has charges that cancel to zero?
column28: MgCl₂: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. MgCl is +2 − 1 = +1, Mg₂Cl is +4 − 1 = +3, and Mg₂Cl₂ is +4 − 2 = +2, so none of those cancel.
column29: For each choice, multiply each subscript by its ion's charge and add.

column9: Calcium is in Group 2 and bromine is in Group 17. Write the formula for calcium bromide: ___
column28: Ca²⁺ (Group 2) and Br⁻ (Group 17): the 2 crosses onto bromine, giving CaBr₂. Check: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0.
column29: Get each charge from its group, then criss-cross. Type the 2 as a plain number if you need to.

column9: Potassium forms K⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻. Which formula is correct for potassium oxide?
column28: The 2 from O²⁻ crosses down onto K: K₂O. Check: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0. KO₂ crossed the wrong way, KO does not balance, and the metal goes first.
column29: Each charge drops down as a subscript on the OTHER ion.

column9: In the name iron(III) chloride, what does the (III) tell you?
column15: The iron ion has a 3+ charge
column16: There are 3 iron atoms in the formula
column28: The Roman numeral is the charge of the metal ion: iron(III) means Fe³⁺. It is not a count of atoms, and it is not a group number.
column29: Is a Roman numeral a count of atoms or a charge?

column9: Which ion does copper(II) stand for?
column28: The Roman numeral is the charge, and metal ions are positive, so copper(II) is Cu²⁺. Cu⁺ would be copper(I).
column29: The II is the size of the charge. Is a metal ion positive or negative?

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻. What is the formula for potassium hydroxide?
column28: K⁺ (+1) and OH⁻ (−1) cancel with one of each: KOH. You only need parentheses when there are 2 or more of a polyatomic ion, and KOH₂ would change the hydroxide ion.
column29: Do the charges cancel with one of each? Then are parentheses needed?

column9: When do you put parentheses around a polyatomic ion in a formula?
column14: Every time a polyatomic ion is in the formula
column15: Only when the polyatomic ion is positive
column16: Only when you need 2 or more of that ion
column17: Never; polyatomic ions do not use parentheses
column28: Parentheses go around a polyatomic ion only when you need 2 or more of it, like Ca(NO₃)₂. With just one, like NaNO₃, no parentheses are needed.
column29: Compare NaOH with Ba(OH)₂. Why does only one of them have parentheses?

column9: To make the charges cancel, you are allowed to change the small numbers inside a polyatomic ion, like changing SO₄ to SO₂.
column28: False. Never change anything inside a polyatomic ion. Change how many of the whole ion you use instead, with parentheses if you need 2 or more.
column29: If you change SO₄ to SO₂, is it still the sulfate ion?

column9: Which elements form ions with a 2+ charge? Select all that apply.
column28: Calcium, barium, and strontium are Group 2 metals, so they form 2+ ions. Sodium (Group 1) is 1+, aluminum (Group 13) is 3+, and chlorine (Group 17) is 1−.
column29: Group 2 metals form 2+ ions. Find each element's group.

column9: Match each element to the ion it forms. Use the group number.
column28: Group 1 = +1 (Li⁺), Group 2 = +2 (Ba²⁺), Group 13 = +3 (Ga³⁺), Group 15 = −3 (P³⁻), Group 16 = −2 (Se²⁻), Group 17 = −1 (Br⁻).
column29: Find each element's group. Metals are positive and nonmetals are negative.

column9: Barium chloride is made of Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. After you criss-cross, what subscript goes after Cl? Type just the number.
column28: The 2 from Ba²⁺ drops down onto chlorine, giving BaCl₂. Check: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0.
column29: Barium's charge crosses down to become chlorine's subscript.

column9: Aluminum forms Al³⁺ and fluorine forms F⁻. Which formula is correct for aluminum fluoride?
column28: The 3 from Al³⁺ crosses onto fluorine: AlF₃. Check: (+3) + 3(−1) = 0. Al₃F crossed the wrong way, AlF does not balance, and Al₃F₃ does not balance either.
column29: How many −1 ions does it take to cancel +3?

column9: The formula for sodium sulfide is Na₂S because two Na⁺ ions are needed to cancel one S²⁻ ion.
column28: True. Each Na⁺ is +1 and S²⁻ is −2, so it takes 2 sodium ions: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0, giving Na₂S.
column29: How many +1 charges cancel one −2 charge?

column9: Type the formula for magnesium phosphide: ___
column28: Mg is Group 2 (Mg²⁺) and P is Group 15 (P³⁻). Criss-cross: the 3 goes to Mg and the 2 goes to P, giving Mg₃P₂. Check: 3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0.
column29: Find each charge from its group number, then criss-cross. Can 3 and 2 be reduced?

column9: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate (sulfate is SO₄²⁻). Which formula is correct?
column28: Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ have the same size charge, so one of each cancels: MgSO₄. Mg₂(SO₄)₂ was not reduced, and Mg(SO₄)₂ and Mg₂SO₄ do not balance.
column29: Compare the two charges. If they are the same size, how many of each do you need?

column9: Gallium is in Group 13 and sulfur is in Group 16. Type the formula for gallium sulfide: ___
column28: Ga³⁺ (Group 13) and S²⁻ (Group 16): criss-cross the 3 and the 2 to get Ga₂S₃. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = +6 − 6 = 0.
column29: Get each charge from its group, then cross each charge onto the other ion.

column9: Chlorate is ClO₃⁻. Type the formula for sodium chlorate: ___
column28: Na⁺ (+1) and ClO₃⁻ (−1) cancel with one of each: NaClO₃. With only one chlorate, no parentheses are needed, and nothing inside the ion changes.
column29: Do +1 and −1 cancel with one of each? If so, do you need parentheses?

column9: What is the formula for iron(II) chloride?
column28: Iron(II) is Fe²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so it takes 2 chlorides: FeCl₂. Check: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. FeCl₃ would be iron(III) chloride.
column29: The Roman numeral is iron's charge. How many −1 ions cancel it?

column9: Type the formula for nickel(II) chloride: ___
column28: Nickel(II) is Ni²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻ (Group 17). The 2 crosses onto chlorine: NiCl₂. Check: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0.
column29: Use the Roman numeral as nickel's charge, then criss-cross.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. What is the formula for sodium phosphate?
column28: Na⁺ and PO₄³⁻: the 3 crosses onto sodium, giving Na₃PO₄. Check: 3(+1) + (−3) = 0. NaPO₄ does not balance, Na(PO₄)₃ crossed the wrong way, and Na₃(PO₄)₃ does not balance: 3(+1) + 3(−3) = −6.
column29: Which ion do you need 3 of to cancel a −3?

column9: In strontium phosphide, how many strontium ions are there for every 2 phosphide ions?
column28: Sr²⁺ (Group 2) and P³⁻ (Group 15). 2 phosphides = 2(−3) = −6, so you need 3 Sr²⁺ = +6. The formula is Sr₃P₂.
column29: Find the total negative charge of 2 phosphide ions. How many +2 ions cancel it?

column9: Calcium is Ca²⁺ and sulfur is S²⁻. Which formula for calcium sulfide is fully reduced?
column28: Criss-cross gives Ca₂S₂, which reduces to CaS. Check: (+2) + (−2) = 0. Ca₂S₂ is the step before reducing, and CaS₂ and Ca₂S do not balance.
column29: After you criss-cross, divide both subscripts by any number they share.

column9: Carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Type the formula for aluminum carbonate: ___
column28: Al³⁺ and CO₃²⁻: criss-cross gives Al₂(CO₃)₃. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Keep carbonate in parentheses because you need 3 of it.
column29: Aluminum's charge comes from Group 13. Protect the carbonate ion with parentheses if you need more than one.

column9: Ammonium sulfate is a common lawn fertilizer. Using NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻, type its formula: ___
column28: NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻: the 2 crosses onto ammonium, so you need 2 ammonium ions: (NH₄)₂SO₄. Check: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0. NH₄₂SO₄ is wrong because it changes the ion.
column29: Which ion do you need 2 of? That one gets parentheses.

column9: What is the formula for manganese(III) oxide?
column28: Manganese(III) is Mn³⁺ and oxide is O²⁻. Criss-cross: Mn₂O₃. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. MnO₃ used the numeral as a subscript, and Mn₃O₂ crossed the wrong way.
column29: Use III as manganese's charge, get oxygen's charge from Group 16, then criss-cross.

column9: Write the formula for iron(III) hydroxide, using OH⁻ for hydroxide. Type it here: ___
column28: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and hydroxide is −1, so you need 3 hydroxides: Fe(OH)₃. Check: (+3) + 3(−1) = 0. FeOH₃ would mean 3 hydrogens but only 1 oxygen.
column29: The Roman numeral gives iron's charge. How many hydroxides cancel it, and do you need parentheses?

column9: Acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻. What is the formula for lead(IV) acetate?
column28: Lead(IV) is Pb⁴⁺ and acetate is −1, so it takes 4 acetates in parentheses: Pb(C₂H₃O₂)₄. Check: (+4) + 4(−1) = 0. PbC₂H₃O₂₄ changed the ion, and Pb(C₂H₃O₂)₂ would be lead(II) acetate.
column29: How many −1 ions cancel +4? Keep the whole acetate ion together in parentheses.

column9: Carbonate is CO₃²⁻. When you write the formula for iron(III) carbonate, what subscript goes on Fe? Type just the number.
column28: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and carbonate is −2. The 2 from carbonate crosses down onto iron: Fe₂(CO₃)₃, so the subscript on Fe is 2. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. The III is iron's charge, not its subscript.
column29: Carbonate's charge crosses down onto iron. The Roman numeral is iron's charge, not its subscript.

column9: Ava and Eli write the formula for lead(IV) sulfide. Ava writes PbS₂. Eli writes Pb₂S₄. Who is right?
column14: Both: the two formulas mean the same thing, so either is fine
column15: Ava: criss-crossing Pb⁴⁺ and S²⁻ gives Pb₂S₄, which reduces to PbS₂
column16: Neither: the formula is PbS₄ because the name says IV
column17: Eli: ionic formulas are never reduced
column28: Lead(IV) is Pb⁴⁺ and sulfide is S²⁻. Criss-cross gives Pb₂S₄; both subscripts share a factor of 2, so it reduces to PbS₂. Check: (+4) + 2(−2) = 0. Ionic formulas are always written fully reduced, and PbS₄ uses the numeral as a subscript.
column29: Criss-cross first. Can the subscripts be divided by the same number?

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻, carbonate is CO₃²⁻, and nitrate is NO₃⁻. Select every name that is matched with its correct formula. Select all that apply.
column28: Correct: Ba₃P₂ (3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0), Al₂(SO₄)₃ (2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0), Cu(NO₃)₂ ((+2) + 2(−1) = 0). Iron(II) oxide reduces to FeO, sodium carbonate is Na₂CO₃, and calcium chloride is CaCl₂.
column29: For each one: find the charges, criss-cross, reduce, and check that the charges cancel. Use prefixes for the covalent one.

column9: Ken wrote CaOH₂ for calcium hydroxide (hydroxide is OH⁻). What is wrong with his formula?
column16: He should have reduced it to CaOH
column17: He left out the parentheses, so the 2 only applies to H; it should be Ca(OH)₂
column28: Ca²⁺ needs two OH⁻ ions. Without parentheses, CaOH₂ means 1 O and 2 H, which changes the hydroxide ion. Ca(OH)₂ makes the 2 multiply both O and H. Calcium is always +2, so it never gets a numeral.
column29: What does the 2 in CaOH₂ apply to? What should it apply to?

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Which name–formula pair is NOT correct?
column28: Potassium phosphate should be K₃PO₄: it takes three K⁺ to cancel one PO₄³⁻. The others are right: Mg₃N₂ (3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0), CoCl₂ ((+2) + 2(−1) = 0), and Li₂O (2(+1) + (−2) = 0).
column29: Check each pair: ionic ones must have charges that cancel; covalent ones come straight from the prefixes.

column9: When you name a binary ionic compound, the name of the nonmetal changes its ending to ___.
column28: The nonmetal keeps its root and gets -ide: chlorine becomes chloride, sulfur becomes sulfide, oxygen becomes oxide.
column29: Compare the element name oxygen with the compound name magnesium oxide.

column9: What is the correct name of KBr?
column28: Metal first, then the nonmetal with -ide: potassium bromide. Ionic names never use prefixes, and potassium (Group 1) is always +1, so it never gets a Roman numeral.
column29: Metal + nonmetal = ionic. Write the metal's name, then change the nonmetal's ending.

column9: Sodium is in Group 1 and sulfur is in Group 16. The name of Na₂S is ___.
column28: Na₂S is sodium sulfide. The 2 comes from the criss-cross, but ionic names do not use prefixes, so it is not "disodium sulfide."
column29: Metal name first, then the nonmetal's root + -ide. Do you need a prefix for an ionic compound?

column9: Magnesium is in Group 2. What is the correct name of MgO?
column28: MgO is magnesium oxide. Magnesium (Group 2) is always +2, so no Roman numeral; it is ionic, so no "mono"; and oxygen becomes oxide.
column29: Is Mg a transition metal? Is MgO ionic or covalent? Those two answers rule out three choices.

column9: Because Na₂O has two sodium atoms, its correct name is disodium oxide.
column28: False. Na₂O is sodium oxide. Na₂O is ionic (metal + nonmetal), and prefixes like di- are only for covalent compounds. The 2 comes from balancing Na⁺ with O²⁻.
column29: Which kind of compound uses prefixes: metal + nonmetal, or two nonmetals?

column9: Nitrogen is in Group 15. Complete the name of Mg₃N₂: magnesium ___
column28: Nitrogen becomes nitride. Nitrogen is one of the exceptions that loses two syllables (nitrogen → nitr- + ide), like oxygen → oxide and phosphorus → phosphide.
column29: Nitrogen is one of the elements that loses more than one syllable before the new ending. Watch out: it is not "nitrate" (that is a polyatomic ion).

column9: Calcium is in Group 2. What is the correct name of CaF₂?
column28: CaF₂ is calcium fluoride. Calcium is always +2, so there is nothing to specify with a Roman numeral, and ionic names never use prefixes like di-.
column29: Group 1, 2, and 13 metals have only one possible charge. Does calcium need a numeral?

column9: Because aluminum is in Group 13, Al₂S₃ is named aluminum(III) sulfide.
column28: False. Al₂S₃ is aluminum sulfide. Aluminum always forms Al³⁺, so a Roman numeral adds nothing. Numerals are only for metals that can have more than one charge (like Fe, Cu, Pb, Sn).
column29: Which metals get Roman numerals: ones with only one possible charge, or ones with more than one?

column9: Which metal needs a Roman numeral in its compound names?
column28: Iron (Fe) is a transition metal that can be Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺, so the name must say which. Na (Group 1), Mg (Group 2), and Al (Group 13) each have only one charge.
column29: Look for the metal in groups 3–12 of the periodic table.

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. What is the correct name of NaNO₃?
column28: NaNO₃ is sodium nitrate. A polyatomic ion keeps its own name with no -ide. Nitride is N³⁻ (a single nitrogen), which is a different ion.
column29: The stem tells you the name of NO₃⁻. Does a polyatomic ion's name change?

column9: Lithium is a Group 1 metal and chlorine is a nonmetal. The name of LiCl is ___.
column28: LiCl is lithium chloride: metal name first, then chlorine → chloride.
column29: Metal first, then change chlorine's ending to -ide.

column9: Oxide is O²⁻. What is the charge on the iron ion in FeO? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: One O²⁻ is −2, so the one iron must be +2 to cancel: (+2) + (−2) = 0. FeO is iron(II) oxide.
column29: The total positive charge has to cancel the total negative charge. How much negative charge is there?

column9: Potassium is in Group 1 and phosphorus is in Group 15. Write the name of K₃P. ___
column28: K₃P is potassium phosphide. Phosphorus loses two syllables before -ide (phosphorus → phosphide). No prefix (not "tripotassium") because it is ionic.
column29: Phosphorus is one of the exceptions that drops more than one syllable before adding -ide.

column9: Aluminum is in Group 13. Write the name of Al₂O₃. ___
column28: Al₂O₃ is aluminum oxide. Aluminum is always +3, so no Roman numeral; ionic, so no prefixes (not "dialuminum trioxide").
column29: Ask two questions: Is it ionic or covalent? Can aluminum have more than one charge?

column9: Bromide is Br⁻. Write the name of SnBr₂, including the Roman numeral. ___
column28: Two Br⁻ give −2, so the one tin is +2: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. SnBr₂ is tin(II) bromide.
column29: Total negative charge = 2 × (−1). What charge must one tin have to cancel it?

column9: Oxide is O²⁻. What is the correct name of PbO₂?
column28: Two O²⁻ give −4, so the one lead is +4: (+4) + 2(−2) = 0. PbO₂ is lead(IV) oxide. "Lead(II)" uses the subscript instead of the charge math, "lead oxide" leaves out the needed numeral, and ionic names never use prefixes.
column29: Multiply the oxide charge by the number of oxides, then figure out what one lead must be.

column9: Oxide is O²⁻. What is the charge on each copper ion in Cu₂O? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: One O²⁻ is −2. Two coppers share +2, so each copper is +1: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0. Cu₂O is copper(I) oxide.
column29: Total negative = −2. Split the matching positive charge evenly between the copper atoms.

column9: Jae says every compound of copper and oxygen is just called "copper oxide." Oxide is O²⁻. What is the correct name of CuO?
column28: One O²⁻ is −2, so the one copper is +2. CuO is copper(II) oxide. Jae's name doesn't work because copper can be +1 or +2, and the numeral tells which. Prefixes are never used for ionic compounds.
column29: Copper can be Cu⁺ or Cu²⁺. Use the oxide charge to decide which one is in CuO.

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻. Calcium is in Group 2. Write the name of Ca(OH)₂. ___
column28: Ca(OH)₂ is calcium hydroxide. The polyatomic ion keeps its name, calcium never needs a numeral, and the 2 is not a prefix.
column29: Metal name first, then the polyatomic ion's name exactly as given.

column9: Carbonate is CO₃²⁻. What is the correct name of K₂CO₃?
column28: K₂CO₃ is potassium carbonate. Ionic names use no prefixes, polyatomic ions keep their names (no -ide), and Group 1 metals never get a numeral.
column29: Check three things: prefixes? ending of the polyatomic ion? does a Group 1 metal need a numeral?

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺. Write the name of NH₄Cl. ___
column28: NH₄Cl is ammonium chloride. Ammonium is the positive polyatomic ion, so it goes first like a metal, and chlorine becomes chloride. It is ionic even though it has no metal.
column29: Ammonium plays the role of the metal. Name it first, then the nonmetal with -ide.

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. Select all compounds whose names need a Roman numeral. Select all that apply.
column28: Tin, nickel, and lead can each form more than one charge (for example Sn²⁺ or Sn⁴⁺), so their names need numerals. Mg (Group 2), Li (Group 1), and Al (Group 13) only form one charge, so they never get a numeral.
column29: Find each metal on the periodic table. Groups 1, 2, and 13 never need a numeral.

column9: Put the steps for naming an ionic compound that contains a transition metal in order.
column14: Write the metal's name followed by its charge as a Roman numeral in parentheses.
column15: Decide it is ionic because it has a metal and a nonmetal.
column16: Write the nonmetal's name with an -ide ending.
column17: Use the nonmetal's total charge to find the metal's charge.
column28: Decide ionic vs covalent first, find the metal's charge with reverse criss-cross, write the metal's name with that charge as a Roman numeral, and finish with the nonmetal + -ide.
column29: You must know which naming system you are using before you write anything, and the Roman numeral sits right after the metal's name.

column9: Oxide is O²⁻. What is the charge on each iron ion in Fe₂O₃? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: Three O²⁻ give 3(−2) = −6. Two irons must total +6, so each iron is +3: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide.
column29: Find the total negative charge first, then divide the matching positive charge among the iron atoms.

column9: Chloride is Cl⁻ and bromide is Br⁻. Match each formula to its name.
column28: Each Cl⁻ or Br⁻ is −1, so the number of anions equals the metal's charge here: PbCl₂ +2, PbCl₄ +4, CuBr +1, CuBr₂ +2.
column29: With one metal atom and −1 anions, count the anions to find the metal's charge.

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. Barium is in Group 2. What is the correct name of Ba(NO₃)₂?
column28: Ba(NO₃)₂ is barium nitrate. Nitrate keeps its name (nitride is N³⁻), barium (Group 2) never gets a numeral, and the 2 outside the parentheses is not a prefix.
column29: Polyatomic ions keep their names. Check whether barium can have more than one charge.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Write the name of Sn₃(PO₄)₄, including the Roman numeral. ___
column28: Four PO₄³⁻ give 4(−3) = −12. Three tins must total +12, so each is +4: 3(+4) + 4(−3) = 0. Sn₃(PO₄)₄ is tin(IV) phosphate (phosphate keeps its name, no -ide).
column29: Total negative charge = number of phosphates × (−3). Divide the matching positive charge by the number of tin atoms.

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the correct name of Fe₂(SO₄)₃?
column28: Three SO₄²⁻ give −6, so two irons total +6 and each is +3: iron(III) sulfate. "iron(II)" copies the subscript, "sulfide" puts -ide on a polyatomic ion, and prefixes are never used for ionic compounds.
column29: Reverse criss-cross: what is the total charge of the sulfates, and how many irons share the matching positive charge?

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the charge on the iron ion in FeSO₄? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: One SO₄²⁻ is −2, so the one iron is +2: (+2) + (−2) = 0. The criss-cross gave Fe₂(SO₄)₂, which reduced to FeSO₄. Since the 2 isn't there, it must have reduced.
column29: Don't assume a missing subscript means a charge of 1. Use the sulfate's charge: what cancels −2?

column9: Oxide is O²⁻. Write the name of SnO₂, including the Roman numeral. ___
column28: Two O²⁻ give −4, so the one tin is +4: (+4) + 2(−2) = 0. SnO₂ is tin(IV) oxide (not tin(II), which would copy the subscript, and not tin dioxide, since ionic names have no prefixes).
column29: Total negative = 2 × (−2). One tin has to cancel all of it.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. What is the charge on each lead ion in Pb₃(PO₄)₂? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: Two PO₄³⁻ give 2(−3) = −6. Three leads total +6, so each is +2: 3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0. Pb₃(PO₄)₂ is lead(II) phosphate.
column29: Multiply the phosphate charge by the number of phosphates, then share that amount among the lead atoms.

column9: Chloride is Cl⁻. Which statement best justifies why FeCl₃ needs a Roman numeral in its name but CaCl₂ does not?
column14: Calcium compounds use prefixes instead, so the name already shows its charge.
column15: Iron can form Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺, so the name must say which one; calcium only forms Ca²⁺.
column16: Iron is a nonmetal, so it follows covalent rules, but calcium is a metal.
column17: FeCl₃ has three chlorines, and the Roman numeral counts the chlorine atoms.
column28: Transition metals like iron have more than one possible charge, so the numeral tells which one (here +3, since 3 Cl⁻ give −3). Calcium (Group 2) is always +2, so there is nothing to specify. The numeral is the metal's charge, not an atom count.
column29: What does a Roman numeral tell you about the metal? Can calcium have more than one charge?

column9: Carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Ben names Co₂(CO₃)₃ "cobalt(II) carbonate" because there are 2 cobalt atoms. Which response is correct?
column14: It is dicobalt tricarbonate, because both subscripts count.
column15: It is cobalt(III) carbonate: −6 from the carbonates is shared by 2 cobalts.
column16: It is cobalt(VI) carbonate, because the carbonates total −6.
column17: Ben is right: the subscript on the metal is the numeral.
column28: 3 CO₃²⁻ = −6. Two cobalts total +6, so each is +3: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Ben used the number of atoms as the charge; cobalt(VI) forgot to divide by the 2 cobalts; prefixes are never used for ionic compounds.
column29: The Roman numeral is the charge of ONE metal ion. Find the total negative charge, then divide by the number of cobalt atoms.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Write the name of Cu₃(PO₄)₂, including the Roman numeral. ___
column28: Two PO₄³⁻ give −6. Three coppers total +6, so each is +2: 3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0. Cu₃(PO₄)₂ is copper(II) phosphate.
column29: Do the charge math: total negative from the phosphates, then divide by the number of copper atoms.

column9: Put the steps for finding the Roman numeral of a transition metal from its formula in order.
column14: Divide the total positive charge by the number of metal atoms.
column15: Identify the anion and its charge.
column16: Write that charge as a Roman numeral after the metal's name.
column17: Multiply the anion's charge by the number of anions to get the total negative charge.
column18: Check the finished name: put the numeral's charge back into the formula and confirm the charges add to zero.
column19: Set the total positive charge equal and opposite to the total negative charge.
column28: Anion charge → total negative charge → total positive must cancel it → divide by the number of metal atoms → write the numeral → ALWAYS double check that the charges sum to zero.
column29: Work backward from the part you know (the anion). The very last step is the double check.

column9: Acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻. What is the charge on the nickel ion in Ni(C₂H₃O₂)₂? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: Two C₂H₃O₂⁻ give 2(−1) = −2, so the one nickel is +2: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. The 2 outside the parentheses counts acetate ions. Ni(C₂H₃O₂)₂ is nickel(II) acetate.
column29: Only the subscript outside the parentheses tells how many acetate ions there are. Ignore the numbers inside the ion.

column9: Sulfide is S²⁻. Cu₂S and CuS can both be named copper sulfide, because they contain the same two elements.
column28: False. In Cu₂S, −2 is shared by 2 coppers, so each is +1: copper(I) sulfide. In CuS, one copper cancels −2, so it is +2: copper(II) sulfide. Different compounds need different names, and the numeral shows the difference.
column29: Do the charge math for the copper in each formula. Are the charges the same?

column9: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Write the name of (NH₄)₃PO₄. ___
column28: (NH₄)₃PO₄ is ammonium phosphate. Both ions are polyatomic, so both keep their names: no -ide, no prefixes, no numeral.
column29: Name the positive ion first, then the negative ion. Both names are given to you, and neither changes.

column9: NaF is added to some toothpastes. What is its correct name?
column28: Metal first, then the nonmetal with -ide: sodium fluoride. Sodium (Group 1) is always +1, so it never gets a numeral, and ionic names never use prefixes.
column29: Name the metal, then change fluorine's ending to -ide.

column9: In the name of an ionic compound, the element oxygen is renamed ___.
column28: Oxygen becomes oxide (MgO is magnesium oxide). Oxygen is one of the elements that drops more than one syllable before -ide.
column29: Think of the name of rust: iron(III) ___.

column9: What is S²⁻ called when it is part of an ionic compound's name?
column28: A single sulfur ion, S²⁻, is sulfide (sulfur + -ide). Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) and sulfite are polyatomic ions with oxygen, so they are different ions.
column29: A one-atom nonmetal ion always ends in -ide.

column9: Match each element to the name it takes as the negative ion in an ionic compound.
column28: Keep the root and add -ide: chlor-ide, ox-ide, nitr-ide, phosph-ide, sulf-ide. Nitrate, phosphate, and sulfate are polyatomic ions, not these.
column29: Every one-atom negative ion ends in -ide.

column9: Potassium, iron, copper, lead: which one is always named WITHOUT a Roman numeral?
column28: Potassium (Group 1) only forms K⁺, so its name never needs a numeral. Iron, copper, and lead can each form more than one charge, so their names always need one.
column29: Groups 1, 2, and 13 have only one possible charge.

column9: Which name matches the formula BaS? (Barium is a Group 2 metal.)
column28: BaS is barium sulfide. Barium is always +2, so no numeral; ionic names have no prefixes; and S alone is sulfide, not sulfate (SO₄²⁻).
column29: Check three things: numeral needed? prefixes allowed? which ending does a single S get?

column9: Some salt substitutes are made of KCl. Potassium is a Group 1 metal. Write the name of KCl. ___
column28: KCl is potassium chloride: metal name first, then chlorine → chloride. No numeral (Group 1) and no prefixes.
column29: Metal first, then change chlorine's ending to -ide.

column9: Pick the correct name for MgI₂, a compound of magnesium (Group 2) and iodine.
column28: MgI₂ is magnesium iodide. The 2 comes from balancing charges, but ionic names never use prefixes, magnesium is always +2 (no numeral), and iodine becomes iodide.
column29: Is MgI₂ ionic or covalent? Does magnesium ever have more than one charge?

column9: Lithium is in Group 1 and phosphorus is in Group 15. What is the correct name of Li₃P?
column28: Li₃P is lithium phosphide. No prefixes in ionic names, no numeral for a Group 1 metal, and a single P is phosphide. Phosphate is the polyatomic ion PO₄³⁻.
column29: A single phosphorus ion gets the -ide ending. Do ionic names use prefixes?

column9: Strontium is in Group 2. Write the name of SrO. ___
column28: SrO is strontium oxide. Strontium is always +2, so no numeral, and SrO is ionic, so no "mono."
column29: Metal name, then oxygen with its -ide ending. Does strontium need a numeral?

column9: Which compound should be named with a Roman numeral?
column28: Copper can be +1 or +2, so CuCl₂ needs a numeral: copper(II) chloride. Calcium, sodium, and aluminum each have only one possible charge, so they never get one.
column29: Look for the metal that can have more than one charge.

column9: Why is CaO named calcium oxide and not calcium monoxide?
column14: Calcium needs a Roman numeral instead
column15: Mono is only used on the first element
column16: Oxygen is a metal, so it does not get a prefix
column17: CaO is ionic, and ionic names never use prefixes
column28: Calcium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so CaO is ionic. Prefixes are only for covalent compounds (two nonmetals). Calcium is always +2, so it does not need a numeral either.
column29: Is CaO ionic or covalent? Which system uses prefixes?

column9: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. Potassium is a Group 1 metal. Write the name of KNO₃. ___
column28: KNO₃ is potassium nitrate. The polyatomic ion keeps its own name (no -ide), and potassium never needs a numeral.
column29: Name the metal, then write the polyatomic ion's name exactly as given.

column9: LiOH contains the hydroxide ion, OH⁻. How should LiOH be named?
column28: LiOH is lithium hydroxide. The polyatomic ion keeps its name, lithium (Group 1) never needs a numeral, and lithium oxide is Li₂O, a different compound.
column29: The stem gives you the name of OH⁻. Does it change?

column9: Doctors use BaSO₄ to take X-ray pictures of the stomach. Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the name of BaSO₄?
column28: BaSO₄ is barium sulfate. Sulfate keeps its name (sulfide is S²⁻ alone), barium (Group 2) never gets a numeral, and ionic names have no prefixes.
column29: Polyatomic ions keep their names. Does a Group 2 metal need a numeral?

column9: Many fertilizers contain NH₄NO₃ (ammonium is NH₄⁺, nitrate is NO₃⁻). Which name is correct?
column28: Both ions are polyatomic, so both keep their names: ammonium nitrate. Nitride is N³⁻ alone, and ammonia (NH₃) is a different substance from the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).
column29: Name the positive ion first, then the negative ion, using the names given.

column9: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Because a polyatomic ion keeps its own name, Na₂SO₄ is sodium sulfate, not sodium sulfide.
column28: True. Polyatomic ions keep their names with no -ide. Sodium sulfide would be Na₂S, which has no oxygen.
column29: What would sodium sulfide's formula be?

column9: Which of these compounds are named WITHOUT a Roman numeral? Select all that apply.
column28: Sodium (Group 1), calcium (Group 2), and aluminum (Group 13) each have only one charge, so NaBr, CaI₂, and AlBr₃ get no numeral. Iron, copper, and lead can have more than one charge, so their names need one.
column29: Find each metal. Groups 1, 2, and 13 never get a numeral.

column9: Bromide is Br⁻. In CoBr₂, what charge must the one cobalt ion have? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: Two Br⁻ give 2(−1) = −2, so the one cobalt is +2: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. CoBr₂ is cobalt(II) bromide.
column29: The positive charge must cancel the total negative charge.

column9: Each bromide ion in FeBr₃ is Br⁻. Which name for FeBr₃ is correct?
column28: Three Br⁻ give −3, so the one iron is +3: iron(III) bromide. Ionic names use numerals, not prefixes, and iron must have a numeral because it can be +2 or +3.
column29: Total negative charge = 3 × (−1). What charge must one iron have?

column9: Copper and iodine form CuI. Iodide is I⁻. Which name shows the right charge on copper?
column28: One I⁻ is −1, so the one copper is +1: copper(I) iodide. Copper can be +1 or +2, so a numeral is required, and ionic names never use prefixes.
column29: One iodide is −1. What charge cancels it?

column9: Cesium is a Group 1 metal. Write the name of CsF. ___
column28: CsF is cesium fluoride: metal first, then fluorine → fluoride. Group 1 metals never get a numeral.
column29: Metal name, then the nonmetal's root + -ide.

column9: Strontium is always +2. Which name is correct for SrCl₂?
column28: SrCl₂ is strontium chloride. A metal with only one possible charge gets no numeral, ionic names have no prefixes, and chlorine becomes chloride.
column29: If a metal only has one charge, is there anything for a numeral to tell you?

column9: Type the name of Ca₃P₂ (calcium is a Group 2 metal): ___
column28: Ca₃P₂ is calcium phosphide. The 3 and 2 come from the criss-cross, but ionic names never use prefixes, and calcium (Group 2) never gets a numeral. Phosphorus → phosphide.
column29: Phosphorus drops more than one syllable before -ide. Do you need prefixes?

column9: PbS is a gray mineral called galena. Using S²⁻ for sulfide, name PbS with its Roman numeral: ___
column28: One S²⁻ is −2, so the one lead is +2: (+2) + (−2) = 0. PbS is lead(II) sulfide. No subscripts does not mean a charge of 1.
column29: What charge on one lead ion cancels −2?

column9: NiO is a green powder. Oxide is O²⁻. Which name fits NiO?
column28: One O²⁻ is −2, so the one nickel is +2: nickel(II) oxide. A missing subscript does not mean +1, nickel needs a numeral, and ionic names have no prefixes.
column29: Don't assume no subscript means a charge of 1. Use oxide's charge.

column9: A blue solid forms in a lab: Cu(OH)₂. With hydroxide as OH⁻, choose its name.
column28: Two OH⁻ give −2, so the one copper is +2: copper(II) hydroxide. Ionic names have no prefixes, and hydroxide keeps its name (copper(II) oxide is CuO).
column29: Count the hydroxide ions outside the parentheses to find the total negative charge.

column9: In SnF₄, four F⁻ ions balance one tin ion. What is the tin ion's charge? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
column28: Four F⁻ give 4(−1) = −4, so the one tin is +4: (+4) + 4(−1) = 0. SnF₄ is tin(IV) fluoride.
column29: Total negative charge = number of fluorides × (−1). One tin must cancel all of it.

column9: Smelling salts contain (NH₄)₂CO₃. Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Which name is correct?
column28: Both ions are polyatomic, so both keep their names: ammonium carbonate. The 2 is not a prefix, carbonate gets no -ide, and ammonium never gets a numeral.
column29: Write the two ion names exactly as given. Do ionic names use prefixes?

column9: Iodide is I⁻. Kai names FeI₂ "iron diiodide." Which response is correct?
column14: It is iron(I) iodide, because there is one iron

column29: Is FeI₂ ionic or covalent? Then find iron's charge from the iodides.

column9: Fe(NO₃)₃ contains three nitrate ions (NO₃⁻). Type its name with the correct Roman numeral: ___
column28: Three NO₃⁻ give 3(−1) = −3, so the one iron is +3: iron(III) nitrate. Nitrate keeps its name.
column29: The 3 outside the parentheses counts nitrate ions. What charge must one iron have to cancel them?

column9: Find the charge on nickel in NiSO₄ (sulfate is SO₄²⁻), then type the compound's full name: ___
column28: One SO₄²⁻ is −2, so the one nickel is +2: nickel(II) sulfate. The criss-cross gave Ni₂(SO₄)₂, which reduced to NiSO₄, so a missing subscript does not mean +1.
column29: Use sulfate's charge, not the missing subscripts, to find nickel's charge.

column9: Co₂O₃ has 2 cobalt ions and 3 oxide ions (O²⁻). What charge does each cobalt ion carry? Type the number only (for +2, type 2).
column28: Three O²⁻ give 3(−2) = −6. Two cobalts must total +6, so each is +3: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Co₂O₃ is cobalt(III) oxide.
column29: Find the total negative charge, then split the matching positive charge between the 2 cobalt atoms.

column9: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻. What is the correct name of Co₃(PO₄)₂?
column28: Two PO₄³⁻ give −6. Three cobalts share +6, so each is +2: cobalt(II) phosphate. Cobalt(III) copies the subscript, prefixes are never used in ionic names, and phosphate keeps its name.
column29: Total negative = 2 × (−3). Divide the matching positive charge by the 3 cobalt atoms.

column9: PbCO₃ was once used to make white paint. Using CO₃²⁻ for carbonate, pick the correct name.
column28: One CO₃²⁻ is −2, so the one lead is +2: lead(II) carbonate. Lead can be +2 or +4, so a numeral is required, and no subscript does not mean +1.
column29: Use carbonate's charge to find lead's charge. Does lead need a numeral?

column9: Hydroxide is OH⁻, nitrate is NO₃⁻, and acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻. For which of these would you have to work out a Roman numeral? Select all that apply.
column28: Manganese, chromium, and cobalt can each have more than one charge, so Mn(OH)₂, Cr(NO₃)₃, and Co(C₂H₃O₂)₂ need numerals: manganese(II) hydroxide, chromium(III) nitrate, cobalt(II) acetate. Strontium (Group 2), sodium (Group 1), and aluminum (Group 13) never get one.
column29: Look only at the metal in each formula. Is it in Group 1, 2, or 13?

column9: Oxide is O²⁻. Liv names MnO₂ "manganese(II) oxide" because of the 2 in the formula. Which response is correct?
column14: It is manganese(IV) oxide: two O²⁻ give −4, so the one manganese is +4

column17: It is manganese(I) oxide, because there is only one manganese

column9: The formula Fe(C₂H₃O₂)₂ has acetate ions (C₂H₃O₂⁻). Type its full name, Roman numeral included: ___
column28: Two acetate ions give 2(−1) = −2, so the one iron is +2: iron(II) acetate. Only the 2 outside the parentheses counts the acetate ions; ignore the numbers inside the ion.
column29: How many acetate ions are there? Use only the subscript outside the parentheses.

column9: Chloride is Cl⁻, bromide is Br⁻, iodide is I⁻, and sulfide is S²⁻. Put these compounds in order from the LOWEST to the HIGHEST charge on the metal ion.
column28: CuCl: Cu is +1. CoS: one S²⁻ is −2, so Co is +2. CrBr₃: 3(−1) = −3, so Cr is +3. SnI₄: 4(−1) = −4, so Sn is +4.
